questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Which one of the following graphs represents the velocity-time $(v - t)$ graph of a small spherical body falling in a viscous liquid?
questions.solution:
When a small spherical body falls in a viscous liquid, it experiences three forces: its weight downwards, buoyant force upwards, and viscous drag force upwards.

The equation of motion is given by:
$mg - F_B - F_v = ma$

Using Stokes' law, $F_v = 6\pi \eta r v$, the equation becomes:
$mg - \dfrac{4}{3}\pi r^3 \sigma g - 6\pi \eta r v = m \dfrac{dv}{dt}$

This can be written in the form:
$\dfrac{dv}{dt} = A - Bv$
where $A$ and $B$ are positive constants.

Integrating with the initial condition $v = 0$ at $t = 0$, we get:
$v(t) = \dfrac{A}{B}(1 - e^{-Bt})$

This equation indicates that the velocity of the body initially increases with time, but the rate of increase (acceleration) continuously decreases. As $t \rightarrow \infty$, the velocity asymptotically approaches a constant maximum value known as the terminal velocity ($v_T = \dfrac{A}{B}$).

The first graph correctly represents this behavior, showing the velocity increasing and eventually leveling off to a constant value.

Answer:

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two spherical soap bubbles of radii $r_1$ and $r_2$ in vaccum coalesce under isothermal condition. The newly formed bubble has a radius $(r)$ given by
questions.solution:
Let $P_1 and P_2$ be the pressures inside the two soap bubbles of radii $r_1 and r_2$ respectively.

Since the bubbles are in vacuum, the external pressure is zero. The pressure inside a soap bubble of radius $r$ is given by $P = \dfrac{4T}{r}$, where $T$ is the surface tension.

The volumes of the bubbles are $V_1 = \dfrac{4}{3}\pi r_1^3 and V_2 = \dfrac{4}{3}\pi r_2^3$.

Under isothermal conditions, the temperature remains constant. The total number of moles of gas is conserved when the bubbles coalesce:

$n_1 + n_2 = n$

Using the ideal gas law $PV = nRT$, we get:

$P_1 V_1 + P_2 V_2 = P V$

Substituting the expressions for pressure and volume:

$\left(\dfrac{4T}{r_1}\right) \left(\dfrac{4}{3}\pi$r_1^3\right) + $\left(\dfrac{4T}{r_2}\right) \left(\dfrac{4}{3}\pir_2^3\right) = \left(\dfrac{4T}{r}\right) \left(\dfrac{4}{3}\pir^3\right)$

$\dfrac{16\pi T}{3}r_1^2 + \dfrac{16\pi T}{3}r_2^2 = \dfrac{16\pi T}{3}r^2$

$r_1^2 + r_2^2 = r²$

$r = \sqrt{r_1^2 + r_2^2}$

Answer: $\sqrt{r_1^2 + r_2^2}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A pipe A is connected with other pipes B and C as shown in the figure. The areas of cross-section of A, B and C are respectively $\alpha, \dfrac{\alpha}{2}$ and $\dfrac{\alpha}{4}$. If the velocities of flow of water through A and B are $10$ m/sec and $6$ m/sec, respectively, then velocity of flow, $V_c$ along C is
questions.solution:
According to the principle of continuity, the total volume of fluid entering a junction per unit time must equal the total volume of fluid leaving the junction per unit time.

Therefore, the rate of flow of water through pipe A is equal to the sum of the rates of flow through pipes B and C:

$A_A V_A = A_B V_B + A_C V_C$

Given the cross-sectional areas and velocities:
$A_A = \alpha$, $V_A = 10$ m/s
$A_B = \dfrac{\alpha}{2}$, $V_B = 6$ m/s
$A_C = \dfrac{\alpha}{4}$, $V_C = ?$

Substituting these values into the continuity equation:

$\alpha \times 10 = \left(\dfrac{\alpha}{2}\right) \times 6 + \left(\dfrac{\alpha}{4}\right) \times V_C$

$10\alpha = 3\alpha + \dfrac{\alpha}{4} V_C$

$7\alpha = \dfrac{\alpha}{4} V_C$

$V_C = 7 \times 4 = 28$ m/s

Thus, the velocity of flow along C is $28$ m/sec.

Answer: $28$ m/sec

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A body of density '$\rho$' is dropped slowly on the surface of a lake of depth $d$. If the density of the water be '$\rho'$' $(\rho' < \rho)$ then the time taken by the body to reach the bottom of the lake is
questions.solution:
Let the volume of the body be $V$.

The downward gravitational force acting on the body is $W = V\rho g$.

The upward buoyant force exerted by the water is $F_B = V\rho' g$.

The net downward force on the body is $F_{net} = W - F_B = Vg(\rho - \rho')$.

The downward acceleration $a$ of the body is given by $a = \dfrac{F_{net}}{m} = \dfrac{Vg(\rho - \rho')}{V\rho} = \dfrac{g(\rho - \rho')}{\rho}$.

Using the second equation of motion $s = ut + \dfrac{1}{2}at^2$ with initial velocity $u = 0$ and distance $s = d$:

$d = \dfrac{1}{2}at^2$

$t = \sqrt{\dfrac{2d}{a}}$

Substituting the value of $a$:

$t = \left[\dfrac{2d\rho}{g(\rho - \rho')}\right]^{\dfrac{1}{2}}$

Answer: $\left[\dfrac{2d\rho}{g(\rho - \rho')}\right]^{\dfrac{1}{2}}$

questions.q: A wooden block is floating on water kept in a beaker. $40 \%$ of the block is above the water surface. Now the beaker is kept inside a lift that starts going upward with acceleration equal to $g / 2$. The block will then
options: float with $10 \%$ above the water surface
fioat with $40 \%$ above the water surface
float with $70 \%$ above the water surface
questions.solution:
The buoyant force acting on an immersed body is equal to the weight of the fluid displaced by it, if the fluid is in rest. In this case, the fluid is accelerating upwards so the buoyant force must also provide the displaced fluid force to accelerate.
Therefore, buoyant force will be \($\mathrm{fV} \rho \mathrm{g}_{\text{eff }}$ where \($\mathrm{V}=$ volume of body and \($\mathrm{f}=$ fraction of volume of body immersed in fluid and \($\mathrm{g}_{\text{eff }}=\mathrm{g}+\mathrm{a}=$1.5 $\mathrm{~g}$.
When fluid is at rest: \($\mathrm{f}=$1-0.4=0.6\), 
so \(0.6 $\mathrm{~V} \rho \mathrm{g}=\mathrm{V} \rho_{\mathrm{b}} \mathrm{g}$where \(\rho_{\mathrm{b}}is the $density of the block. \(\Rightarrow \rho_{\mathrm{b}}$=0.6 \rho .\) In $the second case: \(1.5\mathrm{fV} \rho \mathrm{g}=\mathrm{V} \rho_{\mathrm{b}} \mathrm{g}+\mathrm{V} \rho_{\mathrm{b}} \mathrm{a}=$1.5 $\mathrm{~V} \rho_{\mathrm{b}} \mathrm{g} \Rightarrow \mathrm{f} \rho=\rho_{\mathrm{b}} \Rightarrow \mathrm{f}=$0.6\) Thus, the fraction of immersed volume remains the same.
Body will float with \(40 \%\) of the volume above water surface.

To separate the slides a force of $16 \times 10^{5}$ dyne has to be applied normal to the surfaces. The surface tension of the liquid is (in dyne-cm ^{-1}$ )$
questions.solution: Let, thickness of layer be $x$ So, volume $V=$ Area $\times x \begin{array}{ll}$ V=A $\times$ x & (\because)=2 r) \\ x=V / A \end{array} $2 r=\frac{V}{A} \Rightarrow r=\frac{V}{2 A}$ (i) and $\quad \Delta P=\frac{T}{r}$ We know that $F=\Delta P \times A$ =$\frac{T}{r} \times$ A $\begin{array}{l}$ F=$\frac{T}{\left(\frac{V}{2 A}\right)} \times$ A \\ T=$\frac{F \times V}{2 A^{2}} \end{array} [$ from where $F=16 \times 10^{5}$ dyne $, V=0.04 \mathrm{cm}^{3} \begin{aligned}$ A=20 $\mathrm{cm}^{2}=\frac{16 \times 10^{5} \times 0.04}{2 \times 20^{2}}$\\ =$\frac{8 \times 10^{5} \times 4}{20^{2} \times 100}=\frac{8 \times 10^{5} \times 4}{400 \times 100}$\\ =8 $\times10^{5} \times10^{-4} \text{ and } =80 \mathrm{dyne}$/ $\mathrm{cm}$\\ &=80 $\text{ dyne } \mathrm{cm}^{-1} \end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: To determine the composition of a bimetallic alloy, a sample is first weighed in air and then in water. These weights are found to be $w_{1}$ and $w_{2}$ respectively. If the densities of the two constituents metals are $\rho_{1}$ and $\rho_{2}$ respectively. then the weight of the first metal in the sample is (where $\rho_{w}$ is the density of water)
questions.solution:
By Archimedes' Principle
$$
F=v \rho_{w} g \Rightarrow\left(w_{1}-w_{2}\right) g=v \rho_{w} g
$$
Let, the total volume be $v$ and first metal weight be $x$
$$
\begin{array}{l}
w_{1}-w_{2}=\left(v_{1}+v_{2}\right) \rho_{w} \\
w_{1}-w_{2}=v_{1} \rho_{w}+v_{2} g_{w} \\
w_{1}-w_{2}=\left(\frac{x}{\rho_{1}} \rho_{w}+\frac{w_{1}-x}{\rho_{2}} \rho_{w}\right)
w_{1}-w_{2}=\frac{x \rho_{\mathcal{P}} \rho_{w}+\left(w_{1}-x\right) \rho_{w} \rho_{1}}{\rho_{\jmath} \rho_{2}}
\end{array} \quad\left(\because v=\frac{m}{\rho}\right)
$$
$$
\begin{aligned} w_{1} \rho_{1} \rho_{2}-w_{2} \rho_{1} \rho_{2} &=x \rho_{2} \rho_{w}+w_{1} \rho_{w} \rho_{1}-x \rho_{w} \rho_{1} \\ x\left(\rho_{2}-\rho_{1}\right) \rho_{w} &=\rho_{1}\left[w_{1}\left(\rho_{2}-\rho_{w}\right)-w_{2} \rho_{2}\right] \end{aligned}\\
x=\frac{\rho_{1}}{\rho_{w}\left(\rho_{2}-\rho_{1}\right)}\left[w_{1}\left(\rho_{2}-\rho_{w}\right)-w_{z} \rho_{2}\right]
$$

Then some amount of another immiscible liquid of density $\rho_{2}  \left(\rho_{2} < \rho_{1}\right)$ is added to the liquid in the container so that the cylinder now floats just fully immersed in the liquids with $x_{2}$, fraction of volume of the cylinder inside the liquid of density $\rho_{1}$. The ratio $\rho_{1} / \rho_{2} will be$
questions.solution: The given situation is shown as As the Bouyant force in both the cases are same $\therefore \rho_{1} x_{1} g=\rho_{1} x_{2} g+\rho_{2}\left(1-x_{2}\right) g On solving \quad \frac{\rho_{1}}{\rho_{2}}=\frac{\left(1-x_{2}\right)}{\left(x_{1}-x_{2}\right)}$
